title: Alberta Votes on Whether to Hold a Separation Referendum
summary:
People in Alberta, a province in western Canada, are voting on Monday. They are not deciding right away whether to leave Canada. Instead, they are deciding whether to hold a binding referendum on separating at a later date. A referendum is a vote where citizens decide a question directly.

The vote was called earlier this year by Alberta's leader, Danielle Smith, after a grassroots group gathered about 300,000 signatures on a petition. Another group collected more than 400,000 signatures on a petition against separation. About five million people live in Alberta.

Many people who support separation say the oil-rich province's economy has been held back by the environmental policies of Canada's central government in Ottawa. They say Alberta would keep more of its wealth on its own.

People who want Alberta to stay, including Prime Minister Mark Carney, have called for unity. Opponents warn that a newly independent Alberta would face billions of dollars in debt and that the uncertainty could push jobs and investment away. Polls have suggested most Albertans want to remain in Canada, though the debate itself has been divisive.

A court blocked the pro-separation petition, saying it failed to consult Indigenous First Nations whose land would be affected. First Nations groups have called Smith's decision to let the vote go ahead "undemocratic." Smith opposes separation herself, but she says the process gives residents a chance to have their say.

If voters choose to move ahead, a binding referendum could happen as soon as 2027, Smith has said. Albertans are also voting on nine other questions, several about immigration. Hundreds of thousands of people voted early by mail, and early figures suggested strong turnout.
why_it_matters: Whether a province stays in a country is one of the biggest choices voters can make, and Canada is a close neighbor and partner of the United States. The vote also raises questions about how Indigenous nations are consulted on decisions affecting their land.

keywords.explanation: A province is a large area of a country with its own local government, like a state in the U.S.
A binding referendum is a public vote whose result the government must follow.
A petition is a written request signed by many people asking leaders to take an action.
A grassroots group is started by ordinary people rather than by politicians or big organizations.
First Nations are Indigenous peoples of Canada whose communities lived there long before Canada existed.
Turnout is how many eligible people actually vote in an election.

background_read: Canada is divided into provinces and territories, and each province has its own government and leader, while the national government meets in Ottawa.
Alberta is a western province whose economy depends heavily on oil and gas, so national environmental rules can affect it strongly.
A referendum lets citizens vote directly on a question; Monday's vote only decides whether to start the legal process for a later binding referendum on separation.
Indigenous First Nations have rights connected to their traditional lands, which is why a court said they needed to be consulted.
